title: Mathematics of Finance
outcomes: Explain why interest is charged and compute simple interest, compound interest (any conversion period), depreciation and growth.
Distinguish nominal, effective and real rates and compute the effective rate of interest.
Compute future and present values of annuities regular and annuities due, sinking-fund deposits and loan instalments (EMIs).
Apply present value to leasing, capital expenditure (NPV) and bond valuation, value level and growing perpetuities, and compute CAGR.

meta.exam_tip: Learn A(n, i) and P(n, i) by heart and always decide first whether payments are at the end (regular) or at the beginning (due) of each period. Convert the rate and the number of periods to the compounding period before using any formula.

concepts.title: Interest — why it is charged and the basic terms
body: Interest is the price a borrower pays for using someone else’s money. Lenders charge it because of: time value of money (a rupee today is worth more than a rupee later); opportunity cost (lending gives up other uses of the money); inflation (money loses purchasing power); liquidity preference (people prefer cash in hand); and risk (the borrower may default — riskier borrowers pay a risk premium).
Principal (P): the sum borrowed or invested. Rate of interest: the charge per ₹100 per period, usually per annum. Accumulated amount (A): principal plus interest at the end of the term.
concepts.analogy: Interest is rent for money — just as you pay rent to use someone’s flat, you pay interest to use someone’s rupees.
concepts.work: Every lending, deposit, lease and valuation file a CA reviews starts from these five reasons — they explain why one borrower pays 9% and another 14%.

concepts.title: Simple interest
body: Simple interest is calculated on the original principal only: I = P × n × r (r as a decimal, n in years); A = P(1 + nr).
Rearranged: P = I/(nr), r = I/(Pn), n = I/(Pr). Time in months or days must be converted to years (e.g. 9 months = 0.75 year).
A sum becomes k times when interest = (k − 1)P, so n × r = k − 1. If it doubles in t years at SI, it triples in 2t years.
concepts.analogy: Simple interest is a fixed salary — the same amount every year, no matter how long you work.
concepts.work: Interest on delayed payments, many short-term advances and statutory interest calculations follow simple interest.

concepts.title: Compound interest and conversion period
body: In compound interest, interest is added to the principal at the end of each conversion period, so later interest is earned on earlier interest. A = P(1 + i)ⁿ and CI = A − P, where i = rate per conversion period and n = number of conversion periods.
Conversion period: annual (m = 1), half-yearly (m = 2), quarterly (m = 4), monthly (m = 12). For a nominal annual rate r compounded m times a year for t years: i = r/m and n = mt.
For two years, CI − SI = P r². For n = 1 conversion period CI = SI.
Same formula, other uses: depreciation on reducing balance V = P(1 − r)ⁿ; population or sales growth A = P(1 + r)ⁿ. When the unknown is n, use logarithms: n = log(A/P)/log(1 + i).
concepts.analogy: Compound interest is a snowball rolling downhill — it picks up snow on the snow it already carries.
concepts.work: Fixed-deposit maturity values, loan balances, depreciation under the written-down value method and growth projections in business plans are all compound-interest calculations.

concepts.title: Effective, nominal and real rates
body: The nominal (stated) rate is the annual rate quoted, ignoring how often interest is compounded.

The effective rate is the actual annual rate earned when interest is compounded more than once a year: E = (1 + r/m)ᵐ − 1. It is higher than the nominal rate whenever m > 1 and does not depend on the principal.

The real rate adjusts the nominal rate for inflation. The study material uses: real rate = nominal rate − inflation (so nominal = real + inflation). (The exact relation is (1 + nominal) = (1 + real)(1 + inflation), which gives a slightly lower real rate.)
Comparing offers: convert every quoted rate to its effective rate first. Lenders tend to advertise the nominal rate on loans; deposit schemes tend to advertise the effective yield.
concepts.analogy: The nominal rate is the price on the menu; the effective rate is the bill after service charges; the real rate is what that bill is worth after prices rise.
concepts.work: When a client compares a bank loan at 10.5% monthly rests with another at 10.7% half-yearly, the effective rate settles which is cheaper.

concepts.title: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund
body: An annuity is a series of equal payments (or receipts) made at equal intervals. In an annuity regular (ordinary annuity) each payment is at the end of the period; in an annuity due each payment is at the beginning. (Read every question for when the first payment falls — terminology differs between books.)
Future value of an annuity regular: FV = A × A(n, i), where A(n, i) = [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/i.
Future value of an annuity due = A × A(n, i) × (1 + i), because each payment earns one extra period of interest.
A sinking fund is money set aside by equal periodic deposits to build up a known sum at a future date (e.g. to replace an asset or repay debentures). Deposit = target ÷ A(n, i).
concepts.analogy: An annuity is a SIP: equal instalments at equal gaps. Paying at the start of each month (due) simply gives every instalment one more month to grow.
concepts.work: Debenture redemption funds, asset replacement funds and retirement corpus planning are sinking-fund calculations.

concepts.title: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)
body: Present value of ₹1 due after n periods = (1 + i)⁻ⁿ (the discount factor).
Present value of an annuity regular: PV = A × P(n, i), where P(n, i) = [1 − (1 + i)⁻ⁿ]/i.
Present value of an annuity due = A × [1 + P(n − 1, i)] = A × P(n, i) × (1 + i): the first payment is already at today’s value.

A loan is amortised when equal instalments repay both interest and principal over its term. Instalment = Loan ÷ P(n, i). In each period, interest = rate × opening balance; principal repaid = instalment − interest. The interest part falls and the principal part rises over time.
concepts.analogy: Present value is looking at the future through the wrong end of a telescope — everything looks smaller, and the further away it is, the smaller it looks.
concepts.work: EMI schedules, interest-versus-principal split for income-tax claims and the valuation of rental streams all use P(n, i).

concepts.title: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation
body: Leasing: the owner (lessor) lets the user (lessee) use an asset for a period in return for lease rentals. For the lessor, compare the PV of rentals with the cost of the asset — a higher PV makes the lease favourable. For the lessee, compare the PV of rentals with the purchase price — a lower PV makes leasing preferable.
Capital expenditure (investment decision): compare the PV of the expected cash inflows with the PV of the outflows; invest if inflows are worth more.

Bond valuation: a bond’s value is the PV of its coupon payments (an annuity) plus the PV of the redemption amount, discounted at the investor’s required yield. If the yield is above the coupon rate, the bond sells below face value (at a discount), and vice versa.
concepts.analogy: All three questions are the same question in different clothes: "Is the stream of future rupees worth more than the rupees I give up today?"
concepts.work: Lease-versus-buy advice, capital-budgeting proposals and investment valuation (including Ind AS fair-value work later in the course) use exactly this present-value logic.

concepts.title: Perpetuities — level and growing
body: A perpetuity is an annuity whose payments continue for ever. Its future value cannot be computed, but its present value is finite, and because the capital itself is never paid back, nothing is added for a principal repayment.
Level perpetuity (payments at the end of each period): PV = R/i. If the first payment is made today (perpetuity due), PV = R/i + R.
Growing perpetuity (first payment R one period from now, growing at g per period, with g < i): PV = R/(i − g).
Rate and payment must match the period: monthly payments need a monthly rate.
concepts.analogy: A perpetuity is a fruit tree that never stops bearing: you pay for the tree, not for an infinite pile of fruit.
concepts.work: Endowment funds, preference shares without a redemption date and the terminal value in business valuation use the perpetuity formulas.

concepts.title: Net present value (NPV) technique
body: NPV is a discounted cash-flow method: all cash flows of a project are brought to their value at time 0 using a chosen discount rate, and the outflows are subtracted from the inflows.
NPV = PV of cash inflows − PV of cash outflows (when there is a single initial outlay: PV of net inflows − initial investment).
Discount rate: ideally the return available on the best alternative investment of the same risk; in practice organisations use a minimum required rate or the weighted average cost of capital (WACC).
Steps: estimate net cash flow each year → choose the rate → find the discount factor (1 + i)⁻ᵗ for each year → multiply → add. Decision: NPV > 0 accept; NPV < 0 reject.
concepts.analogy: NPV is a profit figure measured in "today’s rupees" after paying the investors their required return.
concepts.work: Capital-budgeting proposals in companies and project-finance appraisals by banks are judged on NPV.

concepts.title: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) and rate of return
body: CAGR is the constant annual rate that would take a value from its beginning level V₀ to its ending level Vₙ over n years: CAGR = (Vₙ/V₀)^(1/n) − 1.
It smooths out year-to-year swings, so it is preferred to the simple average of yearly growth rates when comparing investments or business metrics (revenue, users, units).
Calculating the rate of return on past investments helps judge how good the investment decisions were and whether to change strategy.
concepts.analogy: CAGR is the steady speed that would have covered the same distance in the same time, however bumpy the actual drive was.
concepts.work: Analysts and CAs quote revenue and profit CAGRs in project reports, valuation notes and equity research.

illustrations.title: Simple interest: amount and rate
illustrations.q: (a) Find the simple interest and amount on ₹48,000 at 9% p.a. for 2 years 6 months. (b) At what rate of simple interest will a sum become three times itself in 16 years?

solution.text: (b) Tripling means interest = 2P. 2P = P × 16 × r → r = 2/16 = 0.125 = 12.5% p.a.

checks.label: rate % for a sum to triple in 16 years (SI)

illustrations.title: Compound interest with different conversion periods
illustrations.q: Find the amount and compound interest on ₹80,000 for 2 years at 12% p.a. when interest is compounded annually, half-yearly, quarterly and monthly.

solution.text: Use A = P(1 + i)ⁿ with i = 12%/m and n = 2m.
The more frequent the compounding, the larger the amount — but the gain shrinks each time the frequency rises.

illustrations.title: CI − SI shortcut and reducing-balance depreciation
illustrations.q: (a) Find the difference between CI and SI on ₹2,50,000 for 2 years at 8% p.a. (b) A machine costing ₹5,00,000 depreciates at 15% p.a. on the reducing balance. Find its value after 3 years.

checks.label: WDV after 3 years at 15% reducing balance

illustrations.title: Effective rate and real rate
illustrations.q: (a) Which is better for a depositor: 10% p.a. compounded quarterly or 10.2% p.a. compounded half-yearly? (b) A deposit yields 9% while inflation is 5.5%. What is the real rate of return?

solution.text: The 10.2% half-yearly option has the higher effective rate, so it is better for the depositor, even though it compounds less often.
(b) Real rate = 9% − 5.5% = 3.5% (the relation used in the study material).

illustrations.q: Kavita deposits ₹20,000 a year for 5 years in a scheme paying 8% p.a. compounded annually. Find the amount at the end of 5 years if the deposits are made (a) at the end of each year; (b) at the beginning of each year.

illustrations.q: A company must repay ₹10,00,000 of debentures after 6 years. How much should it invest at the end of each year at 9% p.a. compounded annually?

illustrations.q: A car loan of ₹6,00,000 at 12% p.a. is to be repaid in 36 equal monthly instalments starting one month from now. Find the EMI and prepare the first two lines of the amortisation schedule.

illustrations.title: Present value of an annuity due
illustrations.q: Office rent of ₹1,20,000 is payable at the beginning of each year for 4 years. Find its present value at 10% p.a.

solution.text: Annuity due for 4 years = first payment today + annuity regular for 3 years. P(3, 0.10) = 2.48685.
Cross-check: 1,20,000 × P(4, 0.10) × 1.10 gives the same answer.

illustrations.title: Leasing and a capital-expenditure decision
illustrations.q: (a) Sunrise Leasing buys equipment for ₹5,00,000 and leases it for 5 years at ₹1,40,000 a year, payable at the end of each year. Its money earns 12% p.a. Is the lease favourable to Sunrise? (b) A machine costing ₹2,00,000 will contribute ₹55,000 at the end of each year for 5 years. Borrowing costs 11% p.a. Should it be bought?

solution.text: (a) PV of rentals = 1,40,000 × P(5, 0.12) = 1,40,000 × 3.60478 = ₹5,04,668.67. This exceeds the cost of ₹5,00,000, so the lease is favourable to the lessor (only just).
(b) PV of contributions = 55,000 × P(5, 0.11) = 55,000 × 3.6959 = ₹2,03,274.34. This exceeds ₹2,00,000, so the machine should be bought.

illustrations.title: Valuing a bond
illustrations.q: A ₹1,000 bond pays a 9% coupon at the end of each year and is redeemed at par after 4 years. What price should an investor pay if she requires a yield of 11%?

solution.text: Value = ₹279.22 + ₹658.73 = ₹937.95 — below par, because the required yield (11%) is above the coupon rate (9%).

illustrations.title: Perpetuities
illustrations.q: At 8% p.a., value (a) ₹60,000 a year for ever, first payment after one year; (b) the same with the first payment today. (c) At 12%, value ₹40,000 next year growing at 5% a year for ever.

illustrations.title: Net present value of a project
illustrations.q: A project costs ₹3,00,000 now and will return ₹1,20,000, ₹1,50,000 and ₹1,00,000 at the end of years 1, 2 and 3. The cost of capital is 12% (PV factors 0.893, 0.797, 0.712). Find the NPV and advise.

solution.text: NPV = −₹2,090, which is negative: the project earns less than 12%, so it should be rejected — even though the undiscounted inflows (₹3,70,000) exceed the cost.

illustrations.title: CAGR of revenue
illustrations.q: A company’s revenue grew from ₹40 crore in 2022 to ₹58.564 crore in 2026. Find the CAGR.

jobs.title: Comparing two loan offers
jobs.situation: Bank A offers a term loan at 10.5% p.a. with monthly rests; Bank B offers 10.7% p.a. with half-yearly rests. The client assumes Bank A is cheaper because its quoted rate is lower.
steps: Bank B is actually slightly cheaper: Bank A’s lower quoted rate is more than offset by monthly compounding.
Also compare processing fees and prepayment charges before recommending.
jobs.takeaway: Always compare loans on effective, not nominal, rates — the lower quoted rate is not always the cheaper loan.
jobs.think: Why does monthly compounding raise the effective cost of Bank A’s loan?
jobs.answer: Interest is added to the balance every month, so interest is charged on interest twelve times a year.

jobs.title: Lease or buy office equipment
jobs.role: Finance manager in a services company
jobs.situation: A server room upgrade costs ₹40,00,000 to buy, or can be leased for ₹12,50,000 a year for 4 years, payable at year-end. The company can borrow at 10%.
steps: Treat the rentals as an annuity regular: PV = 12,50,000 × P(4, 0.10).
Compare with the purchase price ₹40,00,000: leasing is cheaper in present-value terms.
Note qualitative factors — technology obsolescence favours leasing.
jobs.takeaway: For the lessee, lease if the PV of rentals is below the purchase price.
jobs.think: What if rentals were payable at the start of each year?
jobs.answer: Then they form an annuity due: PV = ₹39,62,331.81 × 1.10 = ₹43,58,564.99, which is more than ₹40,00,000 — buying becomes cheaper.

jobs.title: NPV for a capex proposal
jobs.role: Articled assistant helping in a project report
jobs.situation: A client plans a ₹10,00,000 packaging line expected to save ₹2,60,000 a year for 6 years. Its cost of capital is 13%.
steps: Equal annual savings form an annuity regular: PV = 2,60,000 × P(6, 0.13).
NPV = ₹39,362.95 → positive, so the proposal is acceptable.
State assumptions (no scrap value, savings at year-end) in the report.
jobs.takeaway: With equal yearly inflows, NPV is just one annuity factor minus the outlay.
jobs.think: If the cost of capital rose to 16%, would the answer flip?
jobs.answer: P(6, 0.16) ≈ 3.6847, so PV ≈ ₹9,58,000 — below the outlay; NPV turns negative and the proposal would be rejected.

jobs.title: Funding a debenture redemption
jobs.situation: ₹50,00,000 of debentures fall due in 5 years. The board wants equal year-end investments in a fund earning 7%.
steps: Set up a standing instruction and track the fund balance each year against the schedule.
jobs.takeaway: A sinking-fund deposit is a target divided by A(n, i) — not by P(n, i).
jobs.think: Why would using P(n, i) be wrong here?
jobs.answer: P(n, i) values a stream today (used for loans); here we are building up a future sum, so the future-value factor A(n, i) is needed.

mcqs.q: Simple interest on ₹15,000 at 8% p.a. for 3 years is:
mcqs.explain: Simple interest = P × r × t = 15,000 × 8% × 3 = ₹3,600. Interest is charged on the original principal only, every year. The trap is ₹18,600, which is the amount (principal + interest), not the interest; ₹3,895.68 is compound interest, where interest also earns interest. In practice: many personal loans between relatives and some trade-credit arrangements in India still charge simple interest, and a CA computes interest income on them exactly this way for the income-tax return.

mcqs.q: At what rate of simple interest does a sum double in 8 years?
mcqs.explain: A sum doubles when the interest equals the principal. Under simple interest, P × r × 8 = P, so r = 1/8 = 12.5% a year. The trap is 9.05%, which is the compound-interest rate that doubles money in 8 years; 8% simply copies the number of years. In practice: older 'money-doubling' deposit schemes in India were advertised this way, and an adviser must check whether the return is simple or compound.

mcqs.q: A sum doubles in 6 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become three times?
mcqs.explain: Doubling in 6 years means simple interest equal to P accrues in 6 years. To become three times, the interest must be 2P, which takes 2 × 6 = 12 years, since simple interest grows in a straight line. The trap is 18 years, which multiplies 6 by 3 — but the original principal already counts as one of the three times. In practice: this linear growth is why simple-interest deposits fall well behind compounded ones over long horizons, a point financial planners stress to clients.

mcqs.q: Compound interest on ₹10,000 at 10% p.a. for 2 years (annual compounding) is:
mcqs.explain: Compound interest = P[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] = 10,000 × (1.21 − 1) = ₹2,100: ₹1,000 in year 1 plus ₹1,100 in year 2, because year-2 interest is charged on ₹11,000. The trap is ₹2,000, which is simple interest; ₹12,100 is the amount, not the interest. In practice: bank fixed deposits in India compound interest (typically quarterly), so the depositor's interest grows each period as this calculation shows.

mcqs.q: The amount of ₹50,000 after 1 year at 8% p.a. compounded half-yearly is:
mcqs.explain: For half-yearly compounding, use half the rate per period and twice the periods: i = 8%/2 = 4%, n = 2. Amount = 50,000 × (1.04)² = ₹54,080. The trap is ₹54,000, which ignores compounding within the year; ₹54,121.61 uses quarterly compounding (2% for 4 periods). In practice: many Indian bonds and some savings instruments pay or compound interest half-yearly, so the conversion period must match the product's terms.

mcqs.q: The difference between CI and SI on ₹40,000 for 2 years at 5% p.a. is:
mcqs.explain: For 2 years, CI − SI = P × r², because the only extra is interest on the first year's interest. So 40,000 × (0.05)² = ₹100. Check: CI = ₹4,100 and SI = ₹4,000. The trap is ₹4,100, which is the compound interest itself, not the difference. In practice: this small 'interest on interest' gap widens rapidly over time, which is why borrowers should check whether a loan quote is simple or compound.

mcqs.q: The effective rate corresponding to a nominal 12% p.a. compounded monthly is:
mcqs.explain: Effective rate = (1 + i/m)ᵐ − 1 = (1.01)¹² − 1 = 0.1268, i.e. 12.68%. Monthly compounding adds interest on interest within the year. The trap is 12%, which is the nominal rate itself; 12.36% is the effective rate for half-yearly compounding. In practice: credit-card and NBFC loans often quote monthly rates, and a CA converts them to an effective annual rate to compare offers fairly.

mcqs.q: The effective rate corresponding to a nominal 8% p.a. compounded quarterly is:
mcqs.explain: Quarterly compounding at 8% means 2% per quarter for 4 quarters. Effective rate = (1.02)⁴ − 1 = 0.0824, i.e. 8.24%. The trap is 8.16%, which is the effective rate for half-yearly compounding (1.04² − 1); 8% ignores compounding entirely. In practice: bank FDs in India typically compound quarterly, so the effective yield a depositor earns is slightly above the quoted rate.

mcqs.q: A machine costing ₹1,00,000 depreciates at 10% p.a. on the reducing balance. Its value after 2 years is:
mcqs.explain: Reducing-balance depreciation works like compound interest with a negative rate: value = 1,00,000 × (1 − 0.10)² = ₹81,000 (₹90,000 after year 1, then 10% of that). The trap is ₹80,000, which deducts ₹10,000 each year as in the straight-line method. In practice: the written-down value method of the Income-tax Act applies a fixed percentage to the falling block value in the same way.

mcqs.q: A town of 2,00,000 people grows at 2% a year. Its population after 3 years (nearest whole number) is:
mcqs.explain: Population grows like compound interest: 2,00,000 × (1.02)³ = 2,12,241.6, which rounds to 2,12,242. The trap is 2,12,000, which adds 2% of the original each year (simple growth); 2,08,080 stops after 2 years. In practice: municipal planners and FMCG demand forecasters project population and household numbers with exactly this compound-growth formula.

mcqs.q: The annual rate (compounded annually) at which money doubles in 5 years is about:
mcqs.explain: Set (1 + i)⁵ = 2, so i = 2^(1/5) − 1 = 0.1487, i.e. about 14.87%. The trap is 20%, which is the simple-interest answer (100%/5); 15.87% adds a percentage point by mistake. The 'rule of 72' check gives 72/5 ≈ 14.4%, close to the exact figure. In practice: advisers use this to tell a client what annual return is needed to double a lump sum before, say, a child's college admission.

mcqs.q: The future value of an annuity due equals the future value of the corresponding annuity regular:
mcqs.explain: In an annuity due, each payment is made at the start of the period, so every payment earns interest for one extra period compared with a regular annuity. Hence FV(due) = FV(regular) × (1 + i). The trap is 'plus one payment' — that adds one cash flow rather than one period's interest on all of them. In practice: SIPs debited at the start of each month and rent paid in advance are annuities due, worth more than end-of-period equivalents.
mcqs.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcqs.q: The future value of ₹5,000 paid at the end of each year for 3 years at 10% p.a. is:
mcqs.explain: FV of a regular annuity = R × [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/i = 5,000 × 3.31 = ₹16,550. The payments grow to 6,050 + 5,500 + 5,000. The trap is ₹15,000, which simply adds the three payments and ignores interest; ₹18,205 is the annuity-due value. In practice: this is how one projects the maturity value of a recurring deposit or annual PPF contributions made at year-end.
mcqs.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcqs.q: If the ₹5,000 in the previous question were paid at the beginning of each year, the future value would be:
mcqs.explain: When payments are made at the beginning of each year, each earns one extra year's interest: FV(due) = 16,550 × 1.10 = ₹18,205. The trap is ₹16,550, which is the regular (end-of-year) annuity value from the previous question. In practice: an investor who deposits in PPF early in April rather than at year-end earns this extra year of interest — a tip many CAs give clients.
mcqs.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcqs.q: The present value of ₹10,000 received at the end of each year for 3 years at 10% is:
mcqs.explain: PV of a regular annuity = R × [1 − (1 + i)⁻ⁿ]/i = 10,000 × 2.48685 = ₹24,868.52. Each receipt is discounted for 1, 2 and 3 years. The trap is ₹30,000, which ignores the time value of money; ₹27,355.37 is the value if receipts came at the start of each year. In practice: valuers and lenders discount expected rents or instalments this way to find what a stream of future receipts is worth today.
mcqs.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcqs.q: The present value of ₹10,000 received at the beginning of each year for 3 years at 10% is:
mcqs.explain: With receipts at the start of each year, the first is not discounted: PV = 10,000 × [1 + P(2, 0.10)] = 10,000 × 2.73554 = ₹27,355.37 (equivalently the regular PV × 1.10). The trap is ₹24,868.52, which is the end-of-year (regular annuity) value. In practice: lease rentals and insurance premiums payable in advance are annuities due, and an accountant valuing them must use this higher present value.
mcqs.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcqs.q: How much must be invested at the end of each year at 10% p.a. to accumulate ₹1,00,000 in 4 years?
mcqs.explain: A sinking fund builds up a future sum: deposit = target ÷ A(4, 0.10) = 1,00,000 ÷ 4.641 = ₹21,547.08. The trap is ₹31,547.08, which divides by the present-value factor and gives the instalment to repay a ₹1,00,000 loan — a different problem; ₹25,000 ignores interest. In practice: companies set aside sinking-fund deposits to redeem debentures or replace machinery on a known future date.
mcqs.topic: Annuities — regular and due; future value; sinking fund

mcqs.q: The present value of a perpetuity of ₹12,000 a year at 8% is:
mcqs.explain: A perpetuity pays forever, so its present value is R/i = 12,000/0.08 = ₹1,50,000. The trap is ₹96,000, which multiplies by the rate instead of dividing; ₹1,62,000 adds a year's payment to the right answer. In practice: an endowment that must pay a ₹12,000 scholarship every year forever needs a corpus of ₹1,50,000 invested at 8% — exactly how trusts size such funds.

mcqs.q: A cash flow of ₹5,000 next year grows at 4% a year forever. At a 9% discount rate its present value is:
mcqs.explain: A growing perpetuity is valued at R/(i − g), where R is next year's cash flow: 5,000/(0.09 − 0.04) = 5,000/0.05 = ₹1,00,000. The trap is ₹55,556, which ignores growth (5,000/0.09); ₹38,462 adds g to i. In practice: equity analysts value a stable company's dividend stream with this formula (the Gordon growth model), and it requires the discount rate to exceed the growth rate.

mcqs.q: The present value of ₹1 receivable after n years at rate i (compounded annually) is:
mcqs.explain: Compounding ₹1 for n years gives (1 + i)ⁿ, so to find today's value of ₹1 received after n years we reverse it: PV = 1/(1 + i)ⁿ = (1 + i)⁻ⁿ. The trap is (1 + i)ⁿ, which is the future value, not the present value; 1/(1 + ni) is the simple-interest discount. In practice: every discounted cash-flow valuation, from bond pricing to project appraisal, is built from this discount factor.
mcqs.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcqs.q: Under the NPV technique, a project should be accepted when:
options: PV of inflows is less than PV of outflows
mcqs.explain: NPV = present value of inflows − present value of outflows, discounted at the cost of capital. A positive NPV means the project earns more than that cost and adds value, so it should be accepted. The trap is 'PV of inflows is less than PV of outflows', which describes a negative NPV — a project to reject. In practice: Indian companies use NPV in capital budgeting for new plants or machinery, and lenders often ask for the NPV workings in project reports.

mcqs.q: If the nominal rate of return is 10% and inflation is 6%, the real rate of return (as used in the study material) is:
mcqs.explain: As used in the study material, real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation = 10% − 6% = 4%: it shows the growth in purchasing power after inflation. (The exact Fisher figure, 1.10/1.06 − 1, is about 3.77%.) The trap is 16%, which adds inflation instead of subtracting it; 1.67% divides the two rates. In practice: a 7% FD in a year of 6% CPI inflation leaves the saver barely 1% better off in real terms — before tax.

mcqs.q: Revenue rises from ₹100 crore to ₹144 crore in 2 years. The CAGR is:
mcqs.explain: CAGR = (ending/beginning)^(1/n) − 1 = (144/100)^(1/2) − 1 = 1.2 − 1 = 20%. Check: 100 × 1.2 × 1.2 = 144. The trap is 22%, the simple average (44% ÷ 2), which ignores compounding; 44% is the total growth. In practice: listed companies' annual reports and equity research notes quote revenue and profit growth as CAGR, so analysts compute it this way.
mcqs.topic: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) and rate of return

mcqs.q: A zero-coupon bond pays ₹1,000 after 2 years. If the required yield is 10%, its price today is:
mcqs.explain: A zero-coupon bond pays only the face value at maturity, so its price is the present value: 1,000 × (1.1)⁻² = 1,000/1.21 = ₹826.45. The trap is ₹800, which uses simple discounting (deducting 10% twice); ₹909.09 discounts for only one year. In practice: RBI Treasury Bills are zero-coupon instruments sold at a discount, priced exactly this way.
mcqs.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation

mcqs.q: A lessor finds that the present value of lease rentals exceeds the cost of the asset. The lease is:
mcqs.explain: If the present value of the lease rentals exceeds the cost of the asset, the lessor recovers more than the outlay in today's money, so the lease is favourable to the lessor. The trap is 'favourable to the lessee' — the lessee would pay more, in present-value terms, than buying the asset outright. In practice: leasing companies and NBFCs in India set rentals using this present-value test before quoting a lease.
mcqs.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason why lenders charge interest?
mcqs.explain: Interest is charged because of the time value of money, opportunity cost, inflation, liquidity preference and the risk of default. The going-concern assumption is an accounting concept — that a business will continue in the foreseeable future — and has nothing to do with why interest is charged. The tempting wrong pick is liquidity preference, which sounds technical but is a genuine reason. In practice: a bank's lending rate is built from these components, with a risk premium for weaker borrowers.
mcqs.topic: Interest — why it is charged and the basic terms

mcqs.q: For a nominal rate of 12% p.a. compounded quarterly over 3 years, the rate per period and the number of periods are:
mcqs.explain: Divide the nominal rate by the number of conversions a year and multiply the years by it: i = 12%/4 = 3% per quarter, and n = 3 × 4 = 12 quarters. The trap is '3% and 4', which converts the rate but forgets to convert the time; '12% and 3' ignores quarterly compounding altogether. In practice: bank FD maturity calculators in India apply exactly this quarterly rate-and-period conversion.

mcqs.q: A loan of ₹1,00,000 at 10% p.a. is repaid in 2 equal annual instalments (end of year). Each instalment is:
mcqs.explain: An equal instalment (EMI-type) repayment = loan ÷ P(2, 0.10) = 1,00,000 ÷ 1.73554 = ₹57,619.05. Each instalment covers the interest due plus part of the principal. The trap is ₹55,000, which adds simple interest of one year to half the loan; ₹60,500 uses 1.1² on half. In practice: home-loan and car-loan EMIs in India are calculated on exactly this present-value-of-annuity basis.
mcqs.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcqs.q: Given log 2 = 0.3010 and log 1.08 = 0.0334, the time for money to double at 8% p.a. compound interest is about:
mcqs.explain: Set (1.08)ⁿ = 2 and take logs: n = log 2/log 1.08 = 0.3010/0.0334 ≈ 9.01 years. The trap is 12.5 years, which is the simple-interest doubling time (100%/8%). The rule of 72 gives 72/8 = 9 years — a quick check. In practice: advisers use doubling-time estimates to explain to clients how long a long-term investment such as an equity fund or PPF may take to double.

mcqs.q: ₹20,000 grows to ₹23,328 in 2 years with annual compounding. The rate of interest is:
mcqs.explain: (1 + i)² = 23,328/20,000 = 1.1664, so 1 + i = √1.1664 = 1.08 and i = 8%. Check: 20,000 × 1.08² = 23,328. The trap is 8.32%, which divides total growth (16.64%) by 2 — a simple-interest rate. In practice: finding the implied compound rate from start and end values is how an investor checks the real return on a maturity payout from an insurance or deposit scheme.

questions.q: A loan of ₹3,00,000 at 10% p.a. is to be repaid in 3 equal annual instalments, the first at the end of the first year. Find the instalment and prepare the complete repayment (amortisation) schedule.

model.text: The closing balance after year 3 is nil (any paise difference is rounding).

questions.q: A ₹1,000 debenture carries an 8% coupon payable annually and will be redeemed at ₹1,050 at the end of 5 years. Find its value to an investor who requires 10% p.a.

model.text: Coupon = 8% of face value ₹1,000 = ₹80 a year for 5 years. PV = 80 × P(5, 0.10) = ₹303.26.

scheme.pt: Coupon on face value (₹80), treated as annuity

remarks: Coupon is on face value, not on the redemption value — a common slip.
mistakes: Discounting ₹1,000 instead of the redemption amount ₹1,050.
Using the coupon rate as the discount rate.

viva.q: Why do lenders charge interest? Give the reasons.
viva.model: Lenders charge interest because of the time value of money, since a rupee today is worth more than a rupee in future; opportunity cost, because they give up other uses of the money; inflation, which reduces purchasing power; liquidity preference, because people prefer to keep cash; and risk, because the borrower may default.

viva.q: What is the difference between simple interest and compound interest?
viva.model: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal, so it is the same every year. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus the interest already added, so interest is earned on interest. For more than one period, compound interest is therefore higher than simple interest.

viva.q: Distinguish an annuity regular from an annuity due.
viva.model: In an annuity regular each payment is made at the end of the period, so the first payment comes at the end of the first period. In an annuity due each payment is made at the beginning of the period, so the first payment is made immediately. The value of an annuity due equals the value of the annuity regular multiplied by one plus i.

viva.q: What is the effective rate of interest and how is it calculated?
viva.model: The effective rate is the actual annual rate earned when interest is compounded more than once a year. It equals one plus r by m, raised to the power m, minus one, where r is the nominal annual rate and m is the number of compounding periods in a year. It is higher than the nominal rate whenever compounding is more frequent than yearly, and it does not depend on the principal.

viva.model: Net present value discounts all the cash flows of a project to their value today, using the cost of capital or required rate of return as the discount rate. viva.q: How do you value a perpetuity and a growing perpetuity?
viva.model: A perpetuity pays the same amount for ever, so its future value cannot be found but its present value is the payment divided by the interest rate, R by i. For a growing perpetuity, where payments grow at a constant rate g that is less than i, the present value is R divided by i minus g. The original capital is never paid back, so no principal is discounted.

cases.title: Buy or lease a delivery truck
cases.case: Vardhan Logistics needs a truck for five years. It can buy the truck for ₹24,00,000 cash (no scrap value), or lease it for ₹6,60,000 a year payable at the end of each year. The company can borrow at 12% a year compounded annually. The truck is expected to generate net cash inflows of ₹7,00,000 at the end of each year for five years.

mcqs.q: The present value of ₹1 a year for 5 years at 12%, P(5, 0.12), is closest to:
mcqs.explain: P(5, 0.12) = [1 − (1.12)⁻⁵]/0.12 = (1 − 0.56743)/0.12 = 3.6048. It is the sum of the five yearly discount factors at 12%. The trap is 6.3528, which is the future-value factor A(5, 0.12) — compounding instead of discounting. In practice: finance teams keep such annuity factors in a spreadsheet to value any level five-year stream, such as lease rentals or loan EMIs.
mcqs.topic: Present value of annuities; loan amortisation (EMI)

mcqs.q: The present value of the lease rentals is:
mcqs.explain: Rentals are paid at the end of each year, so PV = 6,60,000 × P(5, 0.12) = 6,60,000 × 3.60478 = ₹23,79,152.29. The trap is ₹33,00,000, which adds the five rentals and ignores discounting; ₹26,64,650.57 treats the rentals as payable in advance. In practice: before signing a vehicle lease, a company's finance team discounts the rentals at its borrowing rate to compare with the cash price.
mcqs.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation

mcqs.q: On cost alone, which option should the company choose?
options: Lease — the PV of rentals is below the purchase price
Buy — the purchase price is below the PV of rentals
mcqs.explain: Compare costs in present-value terms: the lease rentals are worth ₹23,79,152.29 today, which is below the ₹24,00,000 cash price, so leasing is cheaper. The trap is 'Buy', which would be right only if the PV of rentals exceeded the purchase price; comparing undiscounted rentals (₹33,00,000) with the price is the classic error. In practice: Indian logistics firms make lease-or-buy decisions this way, often adding tax effects like depreciation and GST later.
mcqs.topic: Applications: leasing, capital expenditure, bond valuation

mcqs.q: The NPV of buying the truck (inflows ₹7,00,000 a year) is:
mcqs.explain: NPV = PV of inflows − cost = 7,00,000 × 3.60478 − 24,00,000 = 25,23,343.34 − 24,00,000 = ₹1,23,343.34. The positive NPV shows the truck is worth acquiring at a 12% cost of money. The trap is ₹25,23,343.34, which is the PV of inflows without deducting the cost; ₹11,00,000 ignores discounting. In practice: project reports submitted to banks for term loans include an NPV statement like this.

mcqs.q: If the lessor quoted 12% a year compounded monthly instead, the effective annual rate would be:
mcqs.explain: Monthly compounding at 12% means 1% per month: effective rate = (1.01)¹² − 1 = 0.1268, i.e. 12.68%. The trap is 12%, the nominal quote itself; 12.36% is the effective rate for half-yearly compounding. In practice: a finance manager compares lease and loan quotes only after converting them to effective annual rates, since a monthly-compounded 12% costs more than an annual 12%.
